By the midpoint theorem, the segment joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle is half the third side.
X and Y are the midpoints of side AB and side BC, so \(XY = \frac{1}{2}AC = \frac{1}{2} \times 9 = 4.5\) cm.
Y and Z are the midpoints of side BC and side AC, so \(YZ = \frac{1}{2}AB = \frac{1}{2} \times 5 = 2.5\) cm.
X and Z are the midpoints of side AB and side AC, so \(XZ = \frac{1}{2}BC = \frac{1}{2} \times 11 = 5.5\) cm.
Hence \(XY = 4.5\) cm, \(YZ = 2.5\) cm and \(XZ = 5.5\) cm.

(i) In \(\square\)MNRL, side ML \(\parallel\) side NR, and side NR lies along side QR of rectangle PQRS, so seg ML \(\parallel\) seg QR.
In rectangle PQRS, side SP \(\parallel\) side RQ, so seg ML \(\parallel\) seg SP as well.
Now in \(\triangle\)RSP, M is the midpoint of side RP (given) and seg ML \(\parallel\) side SP with L on side RS.
By the converse of the midpoint theorem, L is the midpoint of seg SR.
So \(SL = LR\).
(ii) The diagonals of \(\square\)MNRL are seg LN and seg MR, and the diagonals of a rectangle are congruent, so \(LN = MR\).
M is the midpoint of diagonal PR, so \(MR = \frac{1}{2}PR\).
The diagonals of rectangle PQRS are congruent, so \(PR = SQ\).
So \(LN = MR = \frac{1}{2}PR = \frac{1}{2}SQ\).
Hence \(SL = LR\) and \(LN = \frac{1}{2}SQ\).

[Textbook misprint: the book prints 'traingle' for 'triangle' twice in this question, once for \(\triangle\)ABC and once for \(\triangle\)FED. The stem is transcribed exactly as printed. Nothing in the question or its answer turns on the spelling.]

\(\triangle\)ABC is equilateral, so \(AB = BC = AC\).
F and E are the midpoints of side AB and side AC, so by the midpoint theorem \(FE = \frac{1}{2}BC\).
F and D are the midpoints of side AB and side BC, so \(FD = \frac{1}{2}AC\).
E and D are the midpoints of side AC and side BC, so \(ED = \frac{1}{2}AB\).
Since \(AB = BC = AC\), the three halves are equal, so \(FE = ED = FD\).
A triangle with all three sides congruent is equilateral.
Hence \(\triangle\)FED is an equilateral triangle.

Construction: through D draw seg DN \(\parallel\) seg QM, meeting side PR at point N.
Seg PD is a median of \(\triangle\)PQR, so D is the midpoint of side QR.
In \(\triangle\)QMR, D is the midpoint of side QR and seg DN \(\parallel\) seg QM with N on side MR.
By the converse of the midpoint theorem, N is the midpoint of seg MR, so \(MN = NR\).
In \(\triangle\)PDN, T is the midpoint of seg PD (given) and seg TM \(\parallel\) seg DN (because M lies on ray QT and seg DN \(\parallel\) seg QM), with M on side PN.
By the converse of the midpoint theorem, M is the midpoint of seg PN, so \(PM = MN\).
So \(PM = MN = NR\), and \(PR = PM + MN + NR = 3\,PM\).
Hence \(\frac{PM}{PR} = \frac{1}{3}\).
